summary: Pyrantel pamoate is a poorly absorbed anthelmintic used chiefly for pinworm (Enterobius) infection and also for roundworm. It acts locally in the gut as a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker, paralyzing the worms so they are expelled in the stool. It is given as a single weight-based dose and is available over the counter; the whole household is often treated for pinworm.

moa: Pyrantel is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent in susceptible nematodes. It causes persistent activation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the worm's neuromuscular junction, producing spastic (depolarizing) paralysis. The paralyzed worms lose their grip on the intestinal wall and are expelled by normal peristalsis. It also inhibits worm cholinesterases.

preg: Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed and on the advice of a physician; systemic absorption is low but human data are limited.
lact: Systemic absorption is minimal, so excretion into milk is expected to be low; use during breastfeeding only on the advice of a physician.
renal: No specific dose adjustment; the drug is poorly absorbed and acts within the gastrointestinal tract.
hepatic: Use with caution in patients with hepatic disease, as transient mild elevations of liver enzymes (SGOT/AST) have been reported.

pearls: Poorly absorbed - high gut concentrations make it effective with low systemic toxicity
Do not combine with piperazine: the two are pharmacologically antagonistic

Effective against pinworm and roundworm but not against whipworm (Trichuris)
missed: Pyrantel is normally given as a single dose, so a missed-dose schedule does not usually apply. If a repeat dose was advised after 2 weeks and is missed, take it when remembered.
overdose: Overdose may cause exaggerated gastrointestinal effects, headache, dizziness, and drowsiness. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with symptomatic care. Pyrantel and piperazine should not be used together due to antagonism.
